newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: FORMER RESERVE BANK GOVERNOR WANTS BIG ECONOMIC CHANGES
The former Reserve Bank Governor, Bernie Fraser, has called for sweeping changes to economic policy, aimed at reducing unemployment.
He has urged big changes to economic growth targets and to fiscal and monetary policy.
Addressing a business function in Melbourne, Mr Fraser called for an end to the pretence that micro-economic reform, especially industrial reform, will alone solve unemployment.
He says the key is faster economic growth of between four and five per cent per year, compared with the current government target of 3.75 per cent this financial year.
On interest rates, Mr Fraser says the opportunity has been lost to effect a fifth reduction in the past year.
And he says while fiscal policy has in recent years been used to manage the budget deficit that's now under control.
Instead, he says, there are opportunities to use taxation and spending in a targeted way for short term pruposes.
He says Australians may have to accept higher taxes if they want a better society.
DOWNER TO MEET UNG HUOT
The Foreign Minister, Alexander Downer, will have talks next week with Cambodia's newly installed Prime Minister, Ung Huot.
The meeting will take place in Kuala Lumpur at the annual forum held by the ASEAN Foreign Ministers.
Mr Downer has cancelled his scheduled visit to Cambodia next month as inappropriate following the coup.

But the bilateral meeting with Ung Huot will be one of a series with regional Foreign Ministers at the ASEAN conference. While Cambodia's scheduled membership of ASEAN has been frozen, Ung Huot will be attending in his role as Foreign Minister because Cambodia is one of 21 countries taking part in the security dialogue, the ASEAN Regional Forum.
Australia says it will raise concerns about both Cambodia and Burma in the security talks.
Canberra officials say Mr Downer will be seeking a unified approach to Cambodia from ASEAN and other Asia-Pacific Foreign Ministers.
INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES RISE
Industrial disputes over the year to the end of April jumped by 32 percent.
The figures were released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
But Federal Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith says there was a drop in the number of disputes in June, which he credits to the Government's Work Place Relations Act.

Mr Reith says a good example of the legislation's value was yesterday's decision by the Industrial Relations Commission, ordering train drivers to cross the picket line of Hunter Valley miners in New South Wales.
"There's no doubt the company is on the front foot. There's no doubt the union is on the back foot," Mr Reith said.

"The offer that's been made, whether it's accepted individually or collectively is a very good deal for those workers. It's an extra 170 bucks a week. I mean there'd be a very long queue of unemployed people outside that mine if they could get in at 74-thousand bucks a year."
PETER BALDWIN QUITS PARLIAMENT
Senior Federal Labor front-bencher, Peter Baldwin, has announced his resignation from Parliament.
Mr Baldwin, who has represented the inner-city seat of Sydney for 15 years, will leave when Parliament resumes after its winter recess.
Currently Labor's finance spokesman, Mr Baldwin was a Minister for six years holding portfolio's including Social Security and Employment.
He says he believes it's important people not stay too long in politics and the membership of the Parliamentary Labor Party be regularly renewed.
Acting Opposition Leader, Gareth Evans, says Peter Baldwin has always been one of the most widely read and creative political thinkers in the country, and his decision to quit is disappointing.
COAL MINERS DISPUTE GOES BACK TO THE COMMISSION
The coal miners union has reviewed a draft enterprise agreement put forward by the mining company Rio Tinto for workers at the Hunter Valley Number One Coal mine in New South Wales.
Around 400 miners have been striking at the mine since June 10 over their refusal to sign individual enterprise agreements with the company.
The union's Mick Watson says there are still many issues to be resolved and they'll be discussed at a hearing of the Industrial Commission on Monday.
"Our position is that we'll remain solid."

"We're going back to the Commission on Monday with once again our plea to the Commission and to the company to sit down and negotiate properly, which is across the table. And the sooner that happens the sooner we'll be able to get the people back to work," Mr watson said.
ARL SAYS PROGRESS BEING MADE WITH SUPER LEAGUE
The Australian Rugby League says progress is being made in talks with Super League.
But chief executive Neil Whittaker has declined to set a deadline for the end of the talks, aimed at one competition next year.
He says pushing for a deadline is "pointless".
Mr Whittaker concedes the league split could take away the focus from the playoffs this season, and said the start of September would be an ideal time to have a structure in place for 1998.

"September would be a great month if we could have it. You know if we can get things cleared up before the semi-finals then I think that both competitions would enjoy a semi-final series with more support," he said.
KENNETT SAYS SUICIDE RATE A NATIONAL SHAME
Victoria's premier, Jeff Kennett, has described Australia's suicide rate as a national shame, which must be addressed .
A report produced for the Victorian Government, recommends new cars be fitted with devices which detect excessive levels of carbon monoxide, and for Paracetamol to be available only from chemists.
While launching the report into suicide, Mr Kennett raised the prospect of a national help-line similar to 000.
He says serious consideration should be given to a national number which people everywhere, particularly in rural areas, can ring to get immediate advice.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
